The sun is **off to the camera's right-hand side, and high in the sky**. It is
**outside the frame, beyond the right edge**, and it is **behind the plane of the
lens rather than in front of it** — this is a front/side-lit scene, not a backlit
one.

Concretely, if you stood at the tripod and faced the lighthouse:

* **Azimuth:** turn roughly **70°–90° to your right** and you would be looking
  towards the sun. Measured the other way round, the sun sits about 60–100° of arc
  round from the "directly behind my back" direction, towards the right. So it is
  best described as **abeam to the right, and slightly behind the right shoulder** —
  not straight behind you, and definitely not ahead of you.
* **Elevation:** about **50° above the horizon** (the measurements bracket it at
  roughly 45°–60°). High, but well short of overhead.

So: **up and to the right, roughly at right angles to the direction the camera is
pointing, and tipped slightly behind the photographer.**

## How the image shows this

**1. The lighthouse tower is lit on its right and shaded on its left.**
The tower is a square shaft, dressed with pale stone quoins, presenting its near
corner almost straight at the camera. Using the sea horizon (at about y = 546 px)
as a true horizon line and extending the tower's horizontal mouldings to their
vanishing points, the right-hand face is turned about 43° to the right of the
camera and the left-hand face about 47° to the left. The right-hand face is
brilliantly lit — measured luminance 222–250 out of 255, with the red channel
clipping at 255 — while the identically painted left-hand face measures only
115–127. Same render, same distance, same exposure: one is in sunlight, the other
is in shade lit by sky alone. Because the left face (pointing 47° left of the
camera) is fully shaded, the sun must lie **more than about 43° round to the right**
of straight-behind-the-camera.

**2. Hard shadow modelling appears only on right-facing surfaces.**
Under the lantern gallery there is a band of small corbels and a pierced red-brick
parapet. On the right-hand face the corbels are crisply modelled with black cast
shadows and the brickwork glows bright orange-red; on the left-hand face the very
same mouldings are flat, murky and low-contrast, and the brickwork reads dark
maroon. Direct sun on the right, ambient skylight on the left.

**3. Every cast shadow in the picture is thrown to the left of the object that
casts it.** The palm trees in the garden throw their frond shadows onto the wall of
the keeper's house displaced clearly to the **left** and downwards of the crowns
themselves; the sunlit patches of wall survive to the right of each palm and the
shaded patches lie to its left. Shadows point away from the sun, so the sun is on
the right.

**4. The palms are rim-lit on their right-hand side.** The fronds on the right of
each crown carry bright yellow-green highlights while the fronds on the left are
uniformly dark — the light is coming across from the right.

**5. A recessed doorway at the base of the tower has its left inner jamb lit.**
Light entering a recess from the right falls on the left-hand inner reveal, which is
exactly what the picture shows: a bright tan strip on the left inside the dark
opening.

reports the light direction directly, and this one is bright (values up to 252) on
its **upper-right limb** and dark (values 76–105) on its lower left. Fitting a
Lambertian sphere model to the ball's pixels — solving for light azimuth and
elevation together with the sphere's centre and radius — gives a best fit of about

sharply for elevations below 45° or above 65°, and for azimuths that put the sun to
the left or straight behind.

the large palm in front of the keeper's house throws its shadow onto the wall
behind it, displaced about 40 px to the left for about 60 px downwards. That
horizontal-to-vertical ratio of roughly 0.66 corresponds to a solar elevation of
about **50°–57°** (and the small parallax correction, because the palm stands in
front of the wall, only pushes the figure slightly higher, not lower). This agrees
with the sphere fit. Shadows of this length — a bit shorter than the objects
casting them — mean a sun that is high but not near the zenith.

**8. The sun is not in front of the camera.** The faces of the tower and the walls
of the house that are turned towards the lens carry sunlight and sunlit dapple; if
the sun were anywhere ahead of the camera those planes would all be in shadow and
the picture would be contre-jour. There is also no lens flare, no haze bloom
anywhere in the frame, and — decisively — **no glitter path on the sea** at the
left, which is what you would see if the sun were low or ahead across the water.

climbs steadily in brightness from left to right — about 160 → 174 at the top of
the frame, 180 → 192 lower down, 189 → 200 lower still. That forward-scattering
glow brightening towards the right edge points to the sun lying beyond the right
side of the picture.

The light is warm on the masonry and the shadows are strongly directional but not
long, so this is mid-morning or (more likely, given the hazy, heat-flattened sea and
sky) mid-afternoon rather than noon or golden hour. A 50° sun is consistent with a
few hours either side of midday at this latitude.

This is the Cap Spartel lighthouse on the headland west of Tangier, Morocco, with
the Atlantic occupying the left of the frame and the land rising away to the right.

i.e. an afternoon exposure. This last point depends on reading the geography and is
offered with less confidence than the light-and-shadow analysis above, which stands
on its own.

## One-line summary

**Up and to the right, out of frame: about 50° above the horizon and about 70–90°
round to the photographer's right — over the right shoulder rather than ahead, so
the scene is lit across and slightly from behind the camera.**
